questions.question: Q: What were the different purposes of transformation in Greek and Roman myth?
questions.correctAnswer: Punishment (Arachne for hubris), protection (Daphne from Apollo), escape (Io from Hera's wrath), explanation (why spiders weave), and reward (constellations for heroes).

questions.question: Q: How does the myth of Arachne illustrate the danger of hubris?
questions.correctAnswer: Arachne challenged Athena to a weaving contest and either matched or surpassed her. This hubris — a mortal rivalling a god — led to her transformation into a spider.

questions.question: Q: Why was Actaeon's transformation particularly unjust?
questions.correctAnswer: Actaeon accidentally stumbled upon Artemis bathing — he did not intend to see her. Yet he was still transformed into a stag and killed by his own hounds, showing divine power operated regardless of mortal intention.

tests.description: Short-answer practice on Myths of Transformation

questions.question: Q: How does Ovid use metamorphosis as a literary theme?
questions.correctAnswer: Ovid uses transformation as a metaphor for the instability of identity, the power of desire, and the constant change underlying all reality.

questions.question: Q: What does the myth of Daphne and Apollo reveal about divine power?
questions.correctAnswer: It shows that divine desire could threaten mortals, that gods could pursue against a mortal's will, and that other divine intervention was the only escape from a god's power.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How far do transformation myths reveal the power of the gods over mortals? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Transformation myths reveal the overwhelming power of the gods over mortals, but they also expose tensions and ambiguities in that power dynamic. The gods' ability to transform mortals at will demonstrates absolute physical control — they can reshape a human body into a tree, animal or insect with a single word. Daphne becomes a laurel tree to escape Apollo, Io becomes a cow to conceal her from Hera, and Actaeon becomes a stag and is killed by his own hounds. In each case, the mortal loses their human form, voice and identity entirely, showing that the gods could erase personhood itself. The arbitrariness of this power is striking: Actaeon was punished for an accident, Arachne for excellence in her craft, and Io was transformed not for her own actions but because Zeus chose her. However, transformations also reveal limits to divine power. Daphne's transformation into a laurel tree denied Apollo what he wanted — her body — so her metamorphosis was also an act of resistance. Arachne's weaving was so skilful that Athena could not find a flaw, suggesting mortal talent could rival divine ability. Furthermore, some transformations served mortals rather than gods — people were changed to escape suffering or achieve immortality. Overall, transformation myths primarily reveal divine omnipotence, but they also question its justice and suggest that mortal agency, however limited, could still frustrate divine intention.
